teaching_card.title: Attacking Conflicting Viewpoints (Medium)
teaching_card.body: Conflicting-viewpoints passages give two scientists who explain the same observation differently. Before the questions, write a one-line summary of each view: the cause each proposes and the key evidence each cites. Most questions then ask what one scientist would agree with, what both accept, which finding would help one side, or how a new observation changes the balance. Stay inside the passage; your own science knowledge is not the answer.
key_points: Summarize each viewpoint in one line: cause + main evidence.
Agreement questions: the answer restates that scientist's own claim.
Common ground is the shared observation, not either explanation.
Supporting evidence confirms the mechanism that scientist proposed.
A new observation weakens the view whose prediction it contradicts.
teaching_card.worked_example: Scientist 1: impact caused the extinction (iridium layer, crater). Scientist 2: volcanoes did (long eruptions, earlier declines). Both accept the iridium layer. Finding most lava erupted after the layer formed weakens Scientist 2.

screens.title: Map the two views first
screens.body: Read each viewpoint once and jot the proposed cause, the two or three pieces of evidence, and any point where the scientist concedes something to the other side. Those concessions are where 'both would agree' answers hide, and the evidence lists are where 'which finding supports' answers come from.
key_points: Cause, evidence, concessions: three notes per scientist.
Note what each scientist explicitly denies.

screens.title: Would agree / would disagree
screens.body: For 'Scientist 2 would most likely agree that...', the correct choice is a restatement of something Scientist 2 actually said or clearly implied. Wrong choices usually belong to the other scientist or contradict a detail in the passage. Check each choice against the text rather than against what sounds scientifically reasonable.
screens.worked_example: Scientist 2 says zander arrived eight years ago. 'Zander were present for decades' contradicts that, so Scientist 2 would not agree with it.

screens.title: Evidence and new findings
screens.body: A finding supports a view when it confirms that view's mechanism or prediction. A finding weakens a view when it contradicts something the view requires. Ask: what does each scientist predict should be true? Then see which prediction the new observation matches. A finding consistent with both views does not favor either.
key_points: Weaken = contradicts something that view needs to be true.

screens.title: The main difference
screens.body: When asked what the views differ on, rule out anything both accept: the observation being explained, shared facts, and background science. What remains is the disputed cause or mechanism. The correct choice names that dispute; the others are points of agreement dressed up as disagreements.
key_points: Cross out shared facts; the dispute is what is left.
The difference is usually 'which cause,' not 'whether it happened.'
